data.name: Crash Dummy
data.detailed_description:
The evil D-TROIT has kidnapped MIA, the Advisor’s daughter! You might be playing as CID, the simple crash dummy, but CID was also programmed and equipped with everything need to be the hero he always dreamt of.

It’s time set CID on his adventure and to save MIA.

Crash Dummy is a challenging 2D platform game with multiple challenges to test even the most hardened gamer. Blast, burn and freeze your way through each level. Jump long distances and do some stylish ninja action wall-runs in this story-driven adventure with a unique set of endearing characters.

Game’s Features:

  • Fight your way through the unique worlds corrupted by D-TROIT using the power of your fists. If that doesn’t work, Burn, Blast and Freeze them.
  • Show off your moves: CID was upgraded with Ninja Skills allowing him to run walls and disorient foes by performing insane stunts.
  • Leap through entire levels using CID’s Long jump ability.
  • Sneak through security.
  • Climb & Slide for exciting heights.
  • Launch CID’s Panic Attack and destroy all danger at once.
  • Multiple enemy types, each one with their own attacking moves.
  • Full-controller support.

reviews.review:
Right off the bat, the game treats the player to the Unity startup menu. Following that is the finest animation that North Korea has to offer in a cutscene that looks like the scoreboard at the bowling alley when you get a strike, voiced by folks who generally enunciate well. Combining human DNA with servile dummies apparently creates some sort of hybrids, yielding your basic damsel-in-distress story. I really don't know. I assume that the plot makes more sense in the native language and hallucinatory state of the drugs in which it was written, but whatever was intended, it doesn't perfectly translate to English.

	The opening cutscene is the only fully animated part of the story. The rest of the plot is told through the kind of simple dialogue boxes accompanied by still-frame pictures that were standard for GBA games, albeit, littered with typos, accompanying an overall graphical style of early Flash animation.

	To say that controllers are supported for this game is a misnomer. As far as I can tell, a controller is required. The mouse scrolls through the levels in the main menu, but otherwise, both it and the keyboard might as well be broken. I tried setting up keyboard bindings in the Unity menu, but it's a lengthy and sloppy list that for some reason includes 29 axes for each of 16 different hypothetical joysticks. So, yeah. I might be shirking the professionalism of a proper review by not setting up a bind for every item in a list almost 500 items long just to see what happens, but for an obscure game of this cobbled-together quality, I feel safe in saying that a controller is required.

	Even so, it isn't ideally executed. Normally, for 2D platform games that don't heavily feature any sort of momentum (like the sort you'd find in Mario or Sonic), I favor using the D-pad, as I find it preferable to an analog stick for subtle movements in rigid control. Crash Dummy doesn't really have momentum, outside of a combined dash+jump that I'm 99% sure that the developers didn't intend for the player to use, as it cheeses many puzzles and platforming sections. However, I can't really use the D-pad, as the input drags considerably, often keeping me moving nearly a full second after my finger has left the pad. The stick is too precise though, as it also registers minute up and down movements, meant for stealth and swimming, but it's too sensitive relative to the horizontal directions. On land, it can slow the movement right before a jump, screwing up the entire leap, and I find myself deliberately tilting the stick diagonally up to avoid accidentally slowing myself down. In the water, it makes it very difficult to go left or right without also moving vertically, so taking damage from bumping into hazards becomes an inevitability.

	Of course, I say that as though dying in this game actually means anything. It doesn't. When you die, you respawn right where you left off. When you run out of lives and get a game over, you can continue, again, right where you left off. Only in boss battles does it make a difference, where running out of lives means starting the fights over from their beginnings, but those situations are usually so easy that I only first noticed it during the Bigfoot level, the third boss which is  roughly 75% of the way through the game. It isn't so much a boss as it is a platforming gauntlet. Even so, I didn't get the game over screen because of any legitimate challenge. I died because the platforming, the very core of this game, is terribly flawed.

	The inconsistency of the inputs, movements, and hit detection always turns platforming into a harder task than it needs to be. When hanging from a ledge, there is no clear delineation for when the jump button will cause me to either jump up or fall down, even when pressing a specific direction on the stick. If landing on a moving platform from a great height, the animation that locks me in place for "catching my balance" after such a drop doesn't stick me to the platform, which means that it can move out from under my feet while I'm waiting for the animation to finish, and I fall further. The springs are flat-out broken; The ones activated by dashing into them inexplicably don't always work, and the ones that simply bounce me around have some weird properties, sucking me into their centers and forcing me to use them if they aren't given a berth that feels too wide. It's a bunch of little things that add up to an overall irritating experience.

	With how overly precise and yet somehow laggy the controls and movement are, it's also worth talking about the obstacles expected to be overcome with them, which is where I have to partially concede; The level design in Crash Dummy is actually competent, when it works the way it's supposed to work. The stages are lengthy, to be sure, but they are varied enough in themes and gameplay to stand out from one another. The puzzles, when sound in formation, are a suitable way to break up the typical pacing of running right and killing everything in sight. New mechanics, enemies, and weapons are revealed in a piecemeal fashion that could keep the player hungry for more, under ideal circumstances.

	The sound design fits a similar bill. In the title screen and the level select menu, (the only in-game menu,) the theme music sounds like someone trying to recreate a Fatboy Slim song from memory. During the levels, the soundtrack is quite interesting, especially for the ice mountain stage. That really sounds like something you'd hear in Silent Hill or Hitman. However, the music typically has a tendency to just stop playing for no real reason, and otherwise, the audio quality is pretty scuffed overall. Some effects sound muffled, or they skip, or when there's a lot going on, they'll layer on top of each other to quickly reach annoyingly high volume without any real warning.

	Getting through it took me nearly 4 hours, but I mostly credit that time to just how broken Crash Dummy is, and it's often more frustrating than entertaining. Jumping through platforming sections with sometimes razor-thin time limits while wrangling with the slipshod controls and movement, wasting effort and minutes off of my life trying to solve a required puzzle while not realizing that it has become bugged and that I need to restart the level, grappling with the impossibly inconsistent hitboxes of the enemies and the terrain and even the character I'm playing as... Any one of these would be obnoxious on its own. Combined into one game, it's too much to recommend.

	It's unfortunate, because there is a decent platforming game underneath all of its problems, but Crash Dummy's problems are a mile thick, and mostly feel like a lot of rushed oversight. Even within its price range, there are more refined and more entertaining 2D platformers out there, yet it's not even worth talking about the price, considering how overall maddening this game is to play. Save yourself your money and your time.
